Lecture 23

Fourier representation, inversion and standard pairs

We fix the Fourier convention, prove the inversion formula for continuous integrable functions with integrable transforms by Gaussian regularization, and prove a symmetric-cutoff inversion theorem that returns the half-sum at a jump. We derive the standard pairs, introduce cosine and sine transforms, and collect conventions and pairs on one card.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Compute the Fourier transform of a pulse, a Gaussian or an exponential in the convention of the course, and convert it to another convention.
  • Decide which inversion theorem applies to a given function, and state in which sense the inverse integral converges.
  • Evaluate the symmetric-cutoff inverse of a transform at a point of continuity and at a jump.
  • Read a width of a function and of its spectrum (main lobe, root-mean-square width or half-width at half maximum) from a computed pair, and say which measure is used.

GM 35 wrote a periodic function as a Fourier series, a sum of oscillations whose frequencies are the multiples of one fundamental frequency. A pulse, a decaying signal or a wave packet on the whole line has no period. In this lecture we represent such a function by an integral over a continuum of wave numbers, its Fourier transform. We use the nascent deltas and the standing rules for improper integrals of Lecture 22 as tools. The representation is a theorem with hypotheses, not a definition. Along the way we compute the standard pairs: the rectangular pulse with the sine integral of Lecture 20, the Gaussian with the complex Gaussian integral of Lecture 18, and the two-sided and one-sided exponentials with the residues of Lecture 19. The lecture reads in three stages: the convention and the pairs (Sections 23.1–23.3), inversion (Sections 23.4–23.5), and half-line transforms with the card (Sections 23.6–23.7).

23.1 From Fourier series to the Fourier transform

We first fix the class of functions.

Definition 23.1 (Piecewise continuous, piecewise C1C^1C1, integrable). A function f:R→Cf:\R\to\Cf:R→C is piecewise continuous (Lecture 22, in an equivalent form) if every bounded interval [α,β][\alpha,\beta][α,β] has a finite partition such that on each open piece fff has a continuous extension to the closed piece. It is piecewise C1C^1C1 if moreover on each open piece fff is differentiable and f′f'f′ has a continuous extension to the closed piece. A piecewise continuous fff is integrable on R\RR if ∫−∞∞∣f(x)∣ ⁣dx<∞.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\abs{f(x)}\dd x<\infty .∫−∞∞​∣f(x)∣dx<∞.

A complex-valued function is continuous, or integrable, when its real and imaginary parts are, and its integral is the integral of the real part plus i\iui times that of the imaginary part (GM 35). The piecewise C1C^1C1 functions are those of GM 35, without periodicity. The values at the partition points do not affect integrals, and at every point xxx the one-sided limits f(x−)f(x^-)f(x−) and f(x+)f(x^+)f(x+) exist. Lecture 22’s rules I1–I3 apply to this class. It is narrower than the locally integrable functions of Lecture 22: ∣x∣−1/2e−x2\abs x^{-1/2}\ee^{-x^2}∣x∣−1/2e−x2 is locally integrable, but not piecewise continuous on R\RR.

Definition 23.2 (Fourier transform). For fff integrable on R\RR the Fourier transform of fff is the function f^=F ⁣[f]:R→C\widehat f=\FT{f}:\R\to\Cf​=F[f]:R→C given by f^(k)=F ⁣[f](k)=12π∫−∞∞e−ikxf(x) ⁣dx.\widehat f(k)=\FT{f}(k)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd x .f​(k)=F[f](k)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​e−ikxf(x)dx.(23.1) For a function ggg of kkk the inverse transform is F−1 ⁣[g](x)=12π∫−∞∞eikxg(k) ⁣dk,\IFT{g}(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}g(k)\dd k ,F−1[g](x)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxg(k)dk,(23.2) whenever the integral converges in a stated sense.

The variable kkk is the wave number. The forward transform carries e−ikx\ee^{-\iu kx}e−ikx, the inverse carries e+ikx\ee^{+\iu kx}e+ikx, and each carries the factor (2π)−1/2(2\pi)^{-1/2}(2π)−1/2. For a signal f(t)f(t)f(t) in time we use the same formulas with ttt for xxx and the angular frequency ω\omegaω for kkk, with the same signs. The integral (23.1) converges absolutely, because ∣e−ikxf(x)∣=∣f(x)∣\abs{\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)}=\abs{f(x)}​e−ikxf(x)​=∣f(x)∣. Whether the inverse integral (23.2) converges, and whether it returns fff, is the subject of this lecture. The function f^\widehat ff​ is also called the spectrum of fff.

A Fourier series uses the discrete wave numbers knk_nkn​ of a periodic function; a Fourier transform uses a continuum of wave numbers for a function on the whole line. The two are different objects with different normalizations.

Exchanges of limits and integrals below use Lecture 22’s rule I1 (dominated limits, with the parameter form I1(b)) and rule I3 (Fubini–Tonelli); each use names the rule.

23.4 Inversion on a smooth class

The spectrum of the pulse is not integrable, while the Gaussian spectrum decays faster than every power of 1/∣k∣1/\abs k1/∣k∣. For functions whose spectrum is integrable the inverse integral converges absolutely, and it returns the function.

Theorem 23.6 (Fourier inversion). Let fff be continuous and integrable on R\RR, and let f^\widehat ff​ be integrable on R\RR. Then for every x∈Rx\in\Rx∈R f(x)=12π∫−∞∞eikxf^(k) ⁣dk,f(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f(k)\dd k ,f(x)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxf​(k)dk,(23.9) the integral converging absolutely. In other notation, F−1 ⁣[F ⁣[f]]=f\IFT{\FT f}=fF−1[F[f]]=f.

Proof. We insert the Gaussian factor e−εk2/2\ee^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}e−εk2/2 into the inverse integral, exchange the order of integration, and let ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+ on both sides. Fix x∈Rx\in\Rx∈R. For ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 put Iε=12π∫−∞∞eikxe−εk2/2f^(k) ⁣dk.I_\varepsilon=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{\iu kx}\ee^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}\widehat f(k)\dd k .Iε​=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eikxe−εk2/2f​(k)dk.

Step 1: the left side. For each kkk the integrand tends to eikxf^(k)\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f(k)eikxf​(k) as ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+, and its modulus is at most ∣f^(k)∣\abs{\widehat f(k)}​f​(k)​, which is integrable by hypothesis. By rule I1, IεI_\varepsilonIε​ tends to the right side of (23.9).

Step 2: the exchange. 23.5 Piecewise C1C^1C1 functions and jumps

The pulse is not continuous, and its spectrum is not integrable. Example 23.4 nevertheless found the limit of the symmetric-cutoff inverse at every point. The same holds for every integrable piecewise C1C^1C1 function. The proof needs one lemma on oscillating integrals.

The pulse is an instance of Theorem 23.9, with the one-sided limits 111 and 000 at x=ax=ax=a; the theorem does not require f^\widehat ff​ to be integrable.

Theorem 23.9 recovers values at jumps only through a convention. Changing fff at finitely many points does not change f^\widehat ff​, so no inversion formula can recover the value that fff was given at a jump; the symmetric cutoff returns the half-sum. Lecture 25 compares functions and spectra through integrals of squared moduli, which do not see values at finitely many points; such statements differ in kind from the pointwise statement (23.10).

23.6 Cosine and sine transforms

Parity simplifies the transform. If fff is integrable and even, then e−ikx=cos⁡(kx)−isin⁡(kx)\ee^{-\iu kx}=\cos(kx)-\iu\sin(kx)e−ikx=cos(kx)−isin(kx), the term with sin⁡(kx)f(x)\sin(kx)f(x)sin(kx)f(x) is odd in xxx and integrates to zero, and f^(k)=2π∫0∞f(x)cos⁡(kx) ⁣dx,\widehat f(k)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(kx)\dd x ,f​(k)=π2​​∫0∞​f(x)cos(kx)dx, which is even in kkk. If fff is odd, the cosine term integrates to zero, and f^(k)=−i2π∫0∞f(x)sin⁡(kx) ⁣dx,\widehat f(k)=-\iu\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(kx)\dd x ,f​(k)=−iπ2​​∫0∞​f(x)sin(kx)dx, which is odd in kkk. A function given only on the half-line (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) can be extended to an even or to an odd function on R\RR, and the two formulas above become transforms on the half-line.

Definition 23.10 (Cosine and sine transforms). Let ggg be piecewise continuous on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) with ∫0∞∣g(x)∣ ⁣dx<∞\int_0^\infty\abs{g(x)}\dd x<\infty∫0∞​∣g(x)∣dx<∞. Its cosine transform and sine transform are Fc[g](k)=2π∫0∞g(x)cos⁡(kx) ⁣dx,Fs[g](k)=2π∫0∞g(x)sin⁡(kx) ⁣dx\mathcal F_{\mathrm c}[g](k)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty g(x)\cos(kx)\dd x,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm s}[g](k)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^\infty g(x)\sin(kx)\dd xFc​[g](k)=π2​​∫0∞​g(x)cos(kx)dx,Fs​[g](k)=π2​​∫0∞​g(x)sin(kx)dx for k∈Rk\in\Rk∈R.

By the parity formulas, ge^=Fc[g]\widehat{g_{\mathrm e}}=\mathcal F_{\mathrm c}[g]ge​​=Fc​[g] and go^=−iFs[g]\widehat{g_{\mathrm o}}=-\iu\mathcal F_{\mathrm s}[g]go​​=−iFs​[g].

Proposition 23.11 (Inversion on the half-line). Let ggg be piecewise C1C^1C1 on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) (on every bounded subinterval, as in Definition 23.1) with ∫0∞∣g∣ ⁣dx<∞\int_0^\infty\abs g\dd x<\infty∫0∞​∣g∣dx<∞. Then for every x>0x>0x>0 lim⁡R→∞2π∫0RFc[g](k)cos⁡(kx) ⁣dk=lim⁡R→∞2π∫0RFs[g](k)sin⁡(kx) ⁣dk=g(x+)+g(x−)2.\lim_{R\to\infty}\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^R\mathcal F_{\mathrm c}[g](k)\cos(kx)\dd k =\lim_{R\to\infty}\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^R\mathcal F_{\mathrm s}[g](k)\sin(kx)\dd k =\frac{g(x^+)+g(x^-)}2 .R→∞lim​π2​​∫0R​Fc​[g](k)cos(kx)dk=R→∞lim​π2​​∫0R​Fs​[g](k)sin(kx)dk=2g(x+)+g(x−)​. At x=0x=0x=0 the cosine integrals tend to g(0+)g(0^+)g(0+), and the sine integrals are 000.

The first term is odd in kkk, and the second is even, so the symmetric integral equals 2/π∫0RFs[g](k)sin⁡(kx) ⁣dk\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^R\mathcal F_{\mathrm s}[g](k)\sin(kx)\dd k2/π​∫0R​Fs​[g](k)sin(kx)dk. Example 23.12 (Two-sided and one-sided exponentials). We compute three pairs for a>0a>0a>0 and check which inversion theorem applies to each. The basic integral is, for real kkk, ∫0∞e−axe−ikx ⁣dx=1a+ik=a−ika2+k2,\int_0^\infty\ee^{-ax}\ee^{-\iu kx}\dd x=\frac1{a+\iu k}=\frac{a-\iu k}{a^2+k^2},∫0∞​e−axe−ikxdx=a+ik1​=a2+k2a−ik​, by the antiderivative −e−(a+ik)x/(a+ik)-\ee^{-(a+\iu k)x}/(a+\iu k)−e−(a+ik)x/(a+ik), since ∣e−(a+ik)x∣=e−ax→0\abs{\ee^{-(a+\iu k)x}}=\ee^{-ax}\to0​e−(a+ik)x​=e−ax→0. For the one-sided exponential the half-sum at 000 is 12\tfrac1221​, and the symmetric integral at x=0x=0x=0 is 12π∫−RRa−ika2+k2 ⁣dk=12π∫−RRaa2+k2 ⁣dk=1πarctan⁡Ra⟶12,\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{a-\iu k}{a^2+k^2}\dd k=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{a}{a^2+k^2}\dd k=\frac1\pi\arctan\frac Ra\longrightarrow\frac12 ,2π1​∫−RR​a2+k2a−ik​dk=2π1​∫−RR​a2+k2a​dk=π1​arctanaR​⟶21​, as Theorem 23.9 predicts. ◃

F ⁣[e−a∣x∣](k)=2π aa2+k2,F ⁣[sgn⁡(x)e−a∣x∣](k)=−i2π ka2+k2,F ⁣[e−axΘ(x)](k)=12π 1a+ik.\begin{aligned} \FT{\ee^{-a\abs x}}(k)&=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\,\frac a{a^2+k^2},\qquad \FT{\sgn(x)\ee^{-a\abs x}}(k)=-\iu\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\,\frac k{a^2+k^2},\\ \FT{\ee^{-ax}\Heaviside(x)}(k)&=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac1{a+\iu k} . \end{aligned}F[e−a∣x∣](k)F[e−axΘ(x)](k)​=π2​​a2+k2a​,F[sgn(x)e−a∣x∣](k)=−iπ2​​a2+k2k​,=2π​1​a+ik1​.​(23.11)

Amplitude, phase and spectral lines. The spectrum describes a function by the amplitude ∣f^(k)∣\abs{\widehat f(k)}​f​(k)​ and the phase arg⁡f^(k)\arg\widehat f(k)argf​(k) of each wave number. The squared modulus ∣f^(k)∣2\abs{\widehat f(k)}^2​f​(k)​2 is read as the distribution of the energy of the signal over wave numbers; Lecture 25 justifies this reading by Plancherel’s identity. In time, the free motion of the underdamped oscillator of Lecture 9, 0<γ<ω00<\gamma<\omega_00<γ<ω0​, is a combination, with conjugate coefficients, of the exponentials e(−γ±iωd)t\ee^{(-\gamma\pm\iu\omega_{\mathrm d})t}e(−γ±iωd​)t for t>0t>0t>0, with the damping rate γ\gammaγ and the damped frequency ωd\omega_{\mathrm d}ωd​. Each exponential, switched on at t=0t=0t=0, gives one line. The one with +iωd+\iu\omega_{\mathrm d}+iωd​ has the spectrum and squared modulus 12π∫0∞e(−γ+iωd)te−iωt ⁣dt=12π 1γ+i(ω−ωd),12π 1γ2+(ω−ωd)2.\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^\infty\ee^{(-\gamma+\iu\omega_{\mathrm d})t}\ee^{-\iu\omega t}\dd t =\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac1{\gamma+\iu(\omega-\omega_{\mathrm d})},\qquad \frac1{2\pi}\,\frac1{\gamma^2+(\omega-\omega_{\mathrm d})^2} .2π​1​∫0∞​e(−γ+iωd​)te−iωtdt=2π​1​γ+i(ω−ωd​)1​,2π1​γ2+(ω−ωd​)21​. This squared modulus is a Lorentzian line centred at ωd\omega_{\mathrm d}ωd​. It falls to half its maximum at ω=ωd±γ\omega=\omega_{\mathrm d}\pm\gammaω=ωd​±γ, so the damping rate is the half-width of the line at half maximum. The exponential with −iωd-\iu\omega_{\mathrm d}−iωd​ gives the mirror line at −ωd-\omega_{\mathrm d}−ωd​.

Summary

The Fourier transform f^(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf(x) ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd xf​(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf(x)dx of an integrable function is bounded and continuous and tends to zero at infinity. Gaussian regularization and rule I3 prove inversion when the transform is integrable; the sine integral of Lecture 20 and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma prove the symmetric-cutoff inversion with half-sums at jumps. The pulse spectrum, a rescaled sin⁡k/k\sin k/ksink/k, is not integrable. The widths of the pulse and Gaussian spectra are reciprocal to the widths of the functions.

  • Convention: f^(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxf ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{-\iu kx}f\dd xf​(k)=(2π)−1/2∫e−ikxfdx and f(x)=(2π)−1/2∫eikxf^ ⁣dkf(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f\dd kf(x)=(2π)−1/2∫eikxf​dk; the same with ttt and ω\omegaω; conversions on the card.

  • Inversion: if fff is continuous and integrable and f^\widehat ff​ is integrable, the inverse integral converges absolutely to f(x)f(x)f(x) at every xxx; this holds for f∈S(R)f\in\Schwartz(\R)f∈S(R).

  • Jumps: if fff is integrable and piecewise C1C^1C1, lim⁡R→∞(2π)−1/2∫−RReikxf^ ⁣dk=12(f(x+)+f(x−))\lim_{R\to\infty}(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-R}^{R}\ee^{\iu kx}\widehat f\dd k=\tfrac12(f(x^+)+f(x^-))limR→∞​(2π)−1/2∫−RR​eikxf​dk=21​(f(x+)+f(x−)); values at jumps are recovered only through this convention.

  • Pairs: Πa^=2/πsin⁡(ka)/k\widehat{\Pi_a}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\sin(ka)/kΠa​​=2/π​sin(ka)/k; F ⁣[e−x2/(2σ2)]=σe−σ2k2/2\FT{\ee^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}}=\sigma\ee^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}F[e−x2/(2σ2)]=σe−σ2k2/2; F ⁣[e−a∣x∣]=2/π a/(a2+k2)\FT{\ee^{-a\abs x}}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,a/(a^2+k^2)F[e−a∣x∣]=2/π​a/(a2+k2); the transform of an even function is the cosine transform of its restriction to (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), and that of an odd function is −i-\iu−i times the sine transform.

Lecture 24 derives the operational rules of the transform and extends it to tempered distributions, such as constants, sinusoids and the delta.
